straightening-hair-brush.summary: A heated paddle brush that straightens and smooths hair as you brush, giving a sleek style that lasts until the next wash.

quick.overview:
A straightening brush is a heated paddle brush that smooths hair as it passes through, combining a hairbrush with the heated plates of a flat iron. The payoff is straight, sleek, neater-looking hair that is visible straight away.

Heat reshapes hydrogen bonds in the hair so it can be held straight, the same principle as a flat iron; the bonds can re-form with moisture. The first brand-name version, DAFNI, was released in 2015 after a ceramic design was patented in 2013. No dedicated studies of these brushes have been published.
quick.how: People brush section by section through dry hair as a quicker, one-step alternative to a flat iron, often finishing with a smoothing product. The larger heated surface covers more hair per pass, and the style holds until the next wash or until humidity and moisture bring the natural shape back.
quick.risks: Overuse of heated styling tools can cause severe hair damage, and hot surfaces can burn skin or scalp. Fine, bleached or already-damaged hair is more vulnerable to heat.

angle.text: A heated brush straightens and smooths hair as you brush, giving a sleeker, neater style that shows immediately and lasts until the next wash. It works on the same heat principle as a flat iron, with a wider heated surface.

flat-iron-hair-straightener.summary: Heated clamp plates that straighten curls or add waves, giving a sleek styled look that lasts until the next wash.

quick.overview:
A flat iron uses two heated plates to straighten curly or wavy hair, and can also add bends and loose waves. The payoff is a smooth, sleek, styled look that is visible immediately.

Heat lets hydrogen bonds in the hair cortex be reshaped while the hair is held straight; they can re-form when hair gets damp, so the effect is temporary. A lab study with an automated iron found that repeated ironing at 120 to 175 degrees Celsius straightened curly hair irreversibly. Safety research on the tools themselves concerns mainly burns.
quick.how: People work through dry hair in sections, clamping and gliding the plates from root to end, and often use a heat-protectant product beforehand. Results last until the next wash or until moisture and humidity restore the natural shape.
quick.risks: Overuse of heated tools can cause severe hair damage, and hot plates can cause contact burns, including in children. Large studies linking hair straightening to cancers or fibroids mostly concern chemical relaxers rather than heated irons.

angle.text: A flat iron straightens curls or adds waves, producing a sleeker styled look that is visible immediately and lasts until the next wash. Heat reshapes the bonds in the hair, and the article covers heat damage.

hair-dryer-brush-hot-air-brush.summary: A brush with built-in heated airflow that dries and styles in one pass, giving root lift, volume and a smooth blowout.

quick.overview:
A hot air brush is a brush with heated airflow built in, so hair is dried and styled at once. The payoff is a fuller, smoother blowout, with root lift and body that is especially sought on fine hair.

A motor blows heated air through the brush head while the bristles lift and shape the hair. Descriptions come mainly from product testers, who report faster drying than a separate dryer and round brush; no clinical studies have been published.
quick.how: People use it on damp hair, working in sections from roots to ends, replacing a separate dryer and round brush. Styling typically takes one pass per section, and the look lasts until the next wash.
quick.risks: No device-specific safety research was found. The main consideration is heat exposure to hair and scalp, as with other heated styling tools, and hot surfaces can burn.

angle.text: A hot air brush dries and styles hair in one pass, giving volume, root lift and a smooth blowout that is visible right away. Product testers report faster drying than a separate dryer and round brush.

premium-multi-styler.summary: A multi-attachment tool, best known as the Dyson Airwrap, that dries, curls, smooths and adds volume in one device.

quick.overview:
A premium multi-styler is a hair tool with swappable heads that can dry, curl, smooth and add volume. The best-known example is the Dyson Airwrap, and several competitors now sell similar devices. The payoff is a polished, voluminous style from one tool, visible immediately.

The device blows heated air through attachments that wrap, brush or shape the hair. Makers say the airflow lets them style at lower heat than traditional irons; that is a manufacturer claim and no independent trial of it has been published.
quick.how: People use the attachments to dry, then curl or smooth in sections, often as a replacement for a dryer plus curling iron. The look lasts until the hair is next washed or restyled.
quick.risks: As with other heated tools, burns and heat-related hair damage are possible. It is sold as a consumer appliance with no medical regulation, and prices are high. Rival makers have been involved in patent disputes with Dyson.

angle.text: A multi-styler such as the Dyson Airwrap dries, curls, smooths and adds volume with one device, for a polished look that is visible immediately. Makers say airflow styling uses less heat than irons; no independent trial has tested this.

wig-lace-front.summary: A wig with a hand-tied lace hairline that looks like it grows from the skin, giving an instant full head of hair.

quick.overview:
A lace front wig has a thin, skin-toned mesh at the front with hairs tied in by hand, so the hairline appears to grow from the skin. The payoff is an instant full head of hair, used for fashion and to conceal hair loss, including medical hair loss.

The lace blends with the skin at the hairline, and the hair is attached by pins, elastic or skin-safe adhesive. It works while worn and is removable; no trial has tested lace fronts specifically. In looksmaxxing and hair-loss communities, lace fronts are discussed mainly as a way to conceal hairline loss.
quick.how: People choose full-lace or partial-lace versions in French or Swiss lace, trim the lace to the hairline, and secure it with pins, elastic or adhesive. They maintain it like hair with regular care and replace it as it wears.
quick.risks: Adhesives and tight attachment can irritate the scalp. Cost and replacement needs vary with materials. Wigs are not regulated as drugs.

angle.text: A lace front wig gives a full head of hair with a hairline that appears to grow from the skin, visible the moment it is worn. It is removable and used to conceal hairline loss.

hair-system-toupee.summary: A custom non-surgical hairpiece fixed to the scalp that restores a full hairline and density while worn.

quick.overview:
A hair system is a custom-made hairpiece, usually attached with adhesive or tape, that covers or fills in areas of hair loss. The payoff is a full hairline and density that is visible immediately. Toupees have been sold for more than a century and remain one option alongside drugs, transplants and shaving the head.

A base of fine lace or similar material carries natural or synthetic hair and is fixed by adhesive, elastic or by weaving into existing hair. Dermatology literature lists hairpieces among camouflage options for hair loss. No trial has compared hair systems with other options for appearance.
quick.how: Men with hair loss have a piece custom-matched to their hair colour and density, then attach and maintain it on a regular schedule. Pieces need periodic replacement, and some people alternate them with other approaches such as drug treatment or a shaved head.
quick.risks: A 2024 case series reported hair loss in six hair system wearers, and weaving methods are linked to traction alopecia. Pieces need regular care; saltwater, chlorine and some shampoos damage fibres.

angle.text: Men with hair loss use custom hair systems, attached with adhesive or tape, to restore a full hairline and density while worn, visible immediately. They are one of several routes alongside drug treatment, transplants and a shaved head.

electric-shaver-foil-rotary.summary: A motorised shaver with foil or rotary heads for a clean, tidy shave, offered as a lower-irritation alternative to blades.

quick.overview:
An electric shaver cuts hair with moving blades behind a perforated foil or rotary head, so the blades do not touch the skin directly. The payoff is a clean, tidy face or body with less redness than blades, according to mostly manufacturer research.

Foil models are often described as closer-cutting, while rotary models suit some face shapes and beards better. A motor oscillates or rotates the cutters; hairs enter holes or slots and are sheared against the guard. Research on skin comfort is mostly from the cosmetic industry, including a 2016 review on reducing shaving-induced irritation.
quick.how: People shave dry or with a compatible wet-shave mode, using foil or rotary heads depending on their beard and face shape. Skin often needs a period to adjust to electric shaving, and results last until the hair regrows.
quick.risks: Irritation is possible, and case reports describe contact allergy to nickel or fragrance components in shavers. Little independent comparative research exists.

angle.text: A foil or rotary electric shaver gives a clean, tidy shave that is visible immediately, with less redness than blades according to mostly manufacturer research. Foil models are often described as closer-cutting.

cartridge-razor.summary: The standard multi-blade razor with a disposable head, giving a close, clean shave and a smooth, groomed face.

quick.overview:
A cartridge razor clips a disposable multi-blade head onto a handle. It has been the dominant style of razor since the 1970s, and the payoff is a close, clean shave visible right after.

Several blades set in a row cut the hair in successive passes, and the cartridge snaps off when dull. Wilkinson introduced the design in 1970 and Gillette followed in 1971; makers have steadily added blades since. In one 2024 study of 59 men, a three-blade cartridge left more shaving-induced redness than a safety razor.
quick.how: People use it with shaving cream or gel and replace the cartridge when it dulls. Cartridges are proprietary, so buyers stay with their handle's brand, and results last until the hair regrows.
quick.risks: Razor-related redness and irritation were higher with a three-blade cartridge than a safety razor in the 2024 study. Cuts are possible with any razor.

angle.text: The cartridge razor is the standard tool for a close, clean shave, with a smooth groomed face visible right after. In one study of 59 men it left more redness than a safety razor.

straight-razor.summary: The traditional folding open razor for a very close shave and a classic wet-shaving ritual.

quick.overview:
A straight razor is a single steel blade that folds into a handle. It was the standard shaving tool before safety and electric razors, and has seen renewed interest since around 2008. The payoff is a very close shave and a smooth, sharply groomed face.

A very sharp edge, kept aligned by stropping and sharpened by honing, slices hair at the skin surface when drawn at a shallow angle. Commentators cite nostalgia, long-term cost, reduced waste and craftsmanship for its return. No clinical studies compare it with other razors.
quick.how: People use it for traditional wet shaving with lather from soap and a brush, stropping the blade before use and honing it periodically or sending it to a professional. It takes practice to learn the angle and pressure.
quick.risks: Nicks and cuts are the main hazards, especially for beginners. Carbon steel blades rust without care, and some blade styles are fragile or bite.

angle.text: A straight razor gives a very close shave and the ritual of traditional wet shaving, with a smooth, sharply groomed face visible right after. Its use has grown again since about 2008.

shaving-brush.summary: A bristle brush that whips soap into a rich lather and lifts hairs for a smoother, closer wet shave.

quick.overview:
A shaving brush builds lather from soap or cream and spreads it over the beard. The payoff, according to reference works, is a richer lather, lifted hairs and light exfoliation for a smoother, closer shave. Bristles come from badger, boar, horse or synthetic fibre, with silvertip badger the premium grade.

Bristles hold water and whip soap into foam, then lift hairs while spreading lather across the skin. No clinical study of these effects was found.
quick.how: People soak the brush, load it with soap or cream, and work the lather on the face in circles before shaving. Natural and synthetic brushes are rinsed and dried between uses.
quick.risks: A 2018 historical review describes anthrax outbreaks between 1915 and 1924 from contaminated imported brushes, with about 20 percent mortality; horse hair brushes then fell out of use for about a century.

angle.text: Wet shavers use a brush to build lather and apply it, with reference works crediting it with richer lather, lifted hairs and light exfoliation for a closer shave. The result is visible straight away.

shaving-soap-cream.summary: Lubricating soaps, creams, foams and gels that help a razor glide for a cleaner shave with less irritation.

quick.overview:
Shaving soap and cream coat the beard and skin so a razor glides with less friction. They come as bars, tubed creams, aerosol foams and gels, and have existed in some form since ancient Sumer. The payoff described is softer hair, fewer nicks and a cleaner shave.

Soap or surfactant, glycerine and emollients hydrate and soften hair and form a lubricating lather or film between blade and skin. No clinical trial of these products for skin or appearance outcomes was found.
quick.how: Hard soaps and tubed creams are worked into lather with a brush, while foams and gels go on directly. People apply them to the wet face before shaving.
quick.risks: Alcohol-rich products can dry the skin, and aerosol cans use flammable propellants. No studies of product-specific irritation were found.

angle.text: Shaving soaps, creams and gels lubricate the skin so the razor glides, aiming for a cleaner shave with less redness that is visible immediately. They soften hair through hydration and reduce friction.

threading-kit.summary: Twisted-thread hair removal for precise eyebrow and facial shaping, now available as an at-home kit.

quick.overview:
Threading uses a twisted thread to pull rows of fine hairs out at the follicle, mostly to shape eyebrows and clean up facial hair. The payoff is precise, clean, defined brows visible immediately. A kit lets people try the technique at home.

A doubled, twisted cotton or polyester thread is rolled across the skin, trapping hairs and lifting them out at the root. It is an ancient practice that began in the Middle East and South Asia, with a long salon tradition. Hair grows back, so results are temporary. Published research is limited, including a 2009 dermatology review of its complications.
quick.how: People hold the thread by hand, mouth or around the neck, with the mouth method described as fastest and most precise. Most learn from salons or tutorials, and results last until hair regrows.
quick.risks: Pain, skin irritation and other complications have been described in a dermatology review. No controlled trials compare it with waxing or tweezing.

angle.text: Threading pulls fine hairs out at the follicle for precise, clean eyebrow and facial shaping that is visible immediately. A home kit brings the salon technique within reach; the result is temporary.

sugaring-paste.summary: A sugar, water and lemon paste that pulls hair out at the root, leaving smooth skin for weeks as a gentler-feeling alternative to wax.

quick.overview:
Sugaring paste is a sticky mixture, traditionally of sugar, water and lemon juice, applied to the skin and pulled off to remove hair at the root. The payoff is smooth, hair-free skin for weeks on the body or face.

Proponents say the paste grips hair rather than skin, is water-soluble and can be used at room temperature or lightly warmed, and prefer it to wax. The medical literature classes sugaring as epilation, grouped with plucking, threading, waxing, lasers and electrolysis. No trials specifically compare sugaring with waxing.
quick.how: People spread or flick the paste against hair growth and pull it off with the grain, working in small patches. It is used on legs, underarms, face and pubic area, with results that last until hair regrows.
quick.risks: Skin irritation is possible, especially on sensitive skin. Reviews note limited evidence on risks and that studies mostly cover dark hair and fair skin. Some products sold as sugar wax contain wax.

angle.text: Sugar paste removes body and facial hair at the root, leaving smooth skin that is visible right after and lasts for weeks. Users prefer it as a gentler alternative to wax.

hair-growth-inhibitor-lotion.summary: Lotions that slow hair regrowth after shaving or waxing; the prescription ingredient eflornithine has trial data.

quick.overview:
These lotions aim to slow how fast unwanted facial or body hair comes back, so smooth skin lasts longer between shaves. The prescription version, eflornithine cream, is used for facial hair in women and has clinical data behind it.

Eflornithine blocks an enzyme (ornithine decarboxylase) in the follicle, which slows hair growth rather than removing hair. Wikipedia reports that in clinical studies 81% of women showed improvement after twelve months, with the effect beginning around eight weeks. Over-the-counter retardant lotions vary in ingredients and no trials of them were found.
quick.how: People apply the lotion to the area after shaving, waxing or plucking, alongside their normal hair removal routine. The effect is gradual, and removal methods continue to be used.
quick.risks: Acne, stinging, itching and rash are reported with eflornithine. Hair regrows to baseline within about eight weeks of stopping. It is a prescription product.

angle.text: Inhibitor lotions slow follicle regrowth so smooth skin lasts longer between shaves or waxes. The prescription ingredient eflornithine has trial data for facial hair in women; over-the-counter versions vary.

whitening-toothpaste.summary: Everyday toothpaste with stain-lifting extras that brightens a smile within weeks by lightening surface stain.

quick.overview:
Whitening toothpaste uses mild abrasives, stain-loosening chemicals and, in some products, peroxide or a blue pigment to make teeth look lighter. The payoff is a brighter smile as coffee and tea stains lift, at far lower cost than professional bleaching.

The effect is mostly mechanical and chemical removal of surface stains, with some products adding optical pigments. Wikipedia reports daily use typically takes two to four weeks to show, and a 2017 systematic review found nearly all whitening toothpastes reduced surface stain without changing the natural colour of the tooth. A 2025 randomised crossover trial looked at blue covarine toothpastes.
quick.how: People swap it in for regular toothpaste and brush twice daily, often alongside whitening strips or professional treatment. Results show over a few weeks and fade if use stops.
quick.risks: Highly abrasive formulas (measured as RDA) can wear enamel with excessive use, and peroxide products can demineralise teeth at high concentrations. Sensitivity can occur.

angle.text: Whitening toothpaste lifts surface stains from coffee and tea for a brighter-looking smile within weeks. It lightens surface stain rather than the tooth's natural shade, and costs far less than professional bleaching.

mandibular-advancement-device.summary: A custom jaw-forward sleep splint that opens the airway to reduce snoring and apnea, supporting better sleep and a more rested look.

quick.overview:
A mandibular advancement device is a custom mouthpiece worn at night that holds the lower jaw slightly forward to keep the airway open. People with snoring or sleep apnea use it to sleep better, which feeds into a more rested look.

Holding the lower jaw forward widens the airway behind the tongue during sleep. Its evidence is for snoring and obstructive sleep apnea: professional sleep societies recommend it for primary snoring and for people who cannot tolerate CPAP, and a randomised trial compared it with CPAP in severe apnea. No studies in the sources reviewed examine appearance effects.
quick.how: A dentist fits a custom splint that is worn each night, usually after a sleep assessment. People who can't tolerate CPAP often turn to it, and follow-up visits adjust the fit.
quick.risks: Dry mouth, tooth and jaw soreness and lasting changes in how the teeth meet are reported. It is a prescription medical device.

angle.text: A mandibular advancement device keeps the airway open during sleep, cutting snoring and apnea so you sleep better and look more rested. It is a medical device studied for sleep apnea, with no published research on appearance.

orthodontic-retainer.summary: The post-braces appliance that keeps teeth where they were moved, protecting a straightened smile.

quick.overview:
A retainer holds teeth in place after braces or aligners, either as a removable plastic or wire device or a wire bonded behind the front teeth. The payoff is keeping the straight smile you paid to achieve.

Passive pressure or a bonded wire keeps teeth from drifting back, a tendency called relapse, attributed to fibre recoil, soft-tissue pressure and continued growth. Orthodontic reviews emphasise that retention is planned in advance, varies in duration and depends on compliance. Forum claims that retainers help or block jaw and palate growth have not been studied.
quick.how: People wear removable retainers (Hawley or clear plastic) nightly after treatment, or have a wire bonded behind the front teeth. Duration varies and many continue long term.
quick.risks: Poor hygiene can cause decay or gum inflammation; bonded retainers can cause unwanted tooth movement (wire syndrome); removable ones can break or warp.

angle.text: Retainers keep teeth in their new positions after braces or aligners, protecting the straight smile you paid for. Forum claims about changing jaw or palate growth have not been studied.

palatal-expander.summary: A screw-driven device that widens the upper jaw, used in children to correct crossbites and discussed by adults hoping for a broader smile and fuller midface.

quick.overview:
A palatal expander widens the upper jaw by turning a screw in a fixed device, most commonly in children and adolescents aged about 8 to 18, to correct a narrow palate, crossbite and crowding. In looksmaxxing communities, expanders and MARPE are discussed for a broader smile and fuller midface, often alongside mewing.

Screw turns separate the two halves of the palate; new bone fills the gap and a retention period follows. Types include rapid (RME), slow, mini-implant-assisted (MARPE) and surgically assisted (SARPE) expansion. Trials focus on dental and airway outcomes in children; broader facial change in adults has not been tested in the sources reviewed.
quick.how: An orthodontist fits the device and the screw is turned on a set schedule, followed by months of retention. Older patients may use MARPE or surgical versions.
quick.risks: Speech changes, pain, a gap between front teeth, bone thinning and relapse are reported; MARPE and SARPE involve implants or surgery.

angle.text: A palatal expander widens the upper jaw, giving a broader dental arch and smile; in kids it is established orthodontics, and some adults hope for a fuller midface, sometimes alongside mewing. Facial change in adults has not been tested.

orthodontic-headgear-facemask.summary: Strap-on orthodontic appliances that guide jaw growth in children, with the facemask pulling the upper jaw forward for underbites.

quick.overview:
Headgear and facemasks apply outside-the-mouth force to guide jaw growth and correct bites in children. The facemask rests on the forehead and chin and uses elastics to pull the upper jaw forward for underbites, giving a more balanced profile. Looksmaxxers ask about them for a more forward midface.

Straps anchor to the head or neck, and elastics or a frame transmit force to the teeth and jaw. The Cochrane review on Class III malocclusion in children describes the facemask as the most commonly reported non-surgical option, usually attached to an expansion appliance. Published support concerns growing patients rather than adults, including claims about facemasks with MARPE.
quick.how: An orthodontist prescribes it for growing patients, often paired with an expander, with elastics worn many hours a day for months.
quick.risks: Eye injuries, tooth soreness, social stigma and possible airway or facial-growth effects are reported; results depend on many hours of daily wear.

angle.text: Headgear and facemasks guide jaw growth in children, with the facemask pulling the upper jaw forward for a more balanced profile. Published support is in growing patients; adult facial-change claims, including with MARPE, are not covered.

herbst-twin-block-functional-appliance.summary: Orthodontic appliances that hold the lower jaw forward in growing teens with an overbite, adding modest lower-jaw length for a stronger profile.

quick.overview:
The Herbst (fixed) and Twin Block (removable) are functional appliances that hold the lower jaw forward in growing children and teenagers with a Class II overbite. The payoff is a corrected bite and a stronger chin and side profile; in looksmaxxing forums they are discussed as a way to advance a small or recessed lower jaw.

The appliance postures the lower jaw forward. Trials and meta-analyses report a modest average gain in lower-jaw length, around 1.5 to 2 mm or more versus controls, together with tooth movement. A review found about two-thirds of samples showed more than 2 mm of extra lengthening, with larger effects during puberty. How much is skeletal rather than dental remains debated.
quick.how: An orthodontist fits the Herbst, fixed with telescoping rods, or the Twin Block, a removable pair of acrylic plates, during the growth period, typically for months before further orthodontic treatment.
quick.risks: Reported effects include early soreness and chewing difficulty, speech changes with removable plates, and forward tilting of lower front teeth. A 2022 meta-analysis did not support forum claims that they recess the upper jaw.

angle.text: Herbst and Twin Block appliances hold the lower jaw forward in growing teens with an overbite, adding modest lower-jaw length and improving the side profile. Research is mostly in children; adult aesthetic use and home-made versions are not covered.
